title: Unveiling hidden aspects of GPS deployment on wildlife: A multistep and transdisciplinary approach to urban wild boar monitoring
author: Marin, Couderchet
materials: Marking and telemetry tracking are governed exclusively by the French Environmental Code and, by extension, by environmental ethics (Rural Code, Art R214–88; Ministerial action service order DGAL/SDSPA/N2013–8095). However, capturing, handling, and carrying GPS devices may affect animal welfare [14,19,20]. In wild boar, fatal injuries linked to a stress-induced flight reaction have been recorded [21,22], while hyperthermia, either from stress or weather, and myopathy are particular concerns during capture [23]. Stress can lead to modifications in spatiotemporal behaviour post-release, putting animals at increased risk of predation or road collisions (see Step 3). Finally, there is the inconvenience of carrying the equipment. The challenge of maximizing animal welfare is ethical. It is also scientific, as the physiological, cognitive, emotional and health status of the animal affects the quality of research outcomes [15,24]. However, wild animal welfare would still occupy a largely insufficient place in the construction of experimental protocols [25]. One explanation lies in the lack of understanding of the 3R principle among some wildlife managers involved in monitoring programs ([26]; personal observations). Furthermore, while ethics of experimental practices rely on recognizing the sensitivity of animals, reflecting a welfarist view of animal ethics inspired by the works of Peter Singer [27], researchers and managers involved in tracking programs would adopt environmental ethics [26], which center its values on the populations and ecosystems above the integrity of the individual living being. Finally, the 3Rs rule was initially developed to improve the welfare of laboratory animals, and applying it to free-ranging wildlife can be challenging. Consequently, principles guiding monitoring protocols may sometimes prioritize practical considerations over wild animal welfare ([15]; personal observations).

These results contrast with those reported in the literature [51], which show a clear effect of capture on both mobility and activity of wild boar during the first 10 days of tracking. These differences could be due to the method of animal immobilization: general anaesthesia versus manual restraint using a custom-made holding cage followed by rapid on-site release (see Step 1). While manual restraint avoids the immediate and delayed effects of anaesthesia (see Appendix 1), our results suggest that it may induce a longer-lasting reduction in wild boar activity than described in the literature. However, these results should be interpreted with caution. First, our sample includes only 10 animals. Additionally, we lack data on the mobility and activity of these individuals before they were equipped. Furthermore, the discomfort caused by carrying the equipment could add to the stress effects related to capture and restraint.

steps.title: Plan study design and collar settings
steps.instruction: Define the research question, program GPS collars to record a position every 30 min (day and night), and decide that no general anaesthesia will be used during capture.

steps.title: Select capture sites and animal criteria
steps.instruction: Choose urban capture sites (despite operational arguments for rural sites) and set weight thresholds: females ≥ 45 kg, males ≥ 50 kg. Only animals meeting these thresholds will receive GPS collars; all captured individuals will receive ear‑tags.

steps.title: Capture, tag, and collar wild boar
steps.instruction: From 23 Jan 2020 to 11 Mar 2021, capture boars at 14 urban sites using experienced operators and a veterinarian‑supervised holding cage; handle manually (no anaesthesia); determine age by morphological criteria; ear‑tag each animal with a unique ID; fit 1 kg Litetrack Iridium 750 PB GPS collars (Lotek) on adult females (≥ 45 kg) and adult males (≥ 50 kg) only – six adult females and eight adult males were collared – then release the animals immediately in an alert state.

steps.title: Export and correct raw GPS data
steps.instruction: Download raw GPS packets (12 records per transmission) from the Iridium server; each record includes date, time, latitude, longitude, altitude, outside temperature, animal ID, sex, age class, and capture location; create a column indicating observation order; correct the manufacturer’s time stamp (adjust 1–2 h offset for winter/summer time).

substeps.instruction: Format the data in Excel (MO Professional Plus 2019, version 1808).
Conduct spatial processing and mapping in QGIS 3.34.

steps.title: Filter GPS locations by quality
steps.instruction: For each location, retain only those with Dilution of Precision (DOP) ≤ 3.4 (corresponding to ‘ideal’ <1 or ‘good‑to‑moderate’ 1–2) and exclude 2D‑least‑square fixes; this removes 25.8 % of records and yields an average GPS error of 6.6 m (controlled) and 7.0 m (field), with 93.9 % (<15 m) and 98.8 % (<30 m) of controlled data meeting those thresholds, and 89.9 % (<15 m) and 97.6 % (<30 m) of field data meeting them.

steps.title: Determine minimum tracking duration
steps.instruction: Calculate home ranges for each of the 14 tracked boars using Minimum Convex Polygon (MCP 100 %). Analyze the relationship between tracking days and home‑range size; observe that home‑range area stabilises after ≈ 12 days and that statistical tests show no significant effect beyond 12 days. Choose a conservative minimum monitoring period of 54 days, which retains 10 individuals (total 1 381 tracking days) for further analysis.

steps.title: Analyze capture‑effect movement metrics
steps.instruction: For the first 50 days of each animal’s tracking, compute: Daily Distance Travelled (DDT, m), Speed per 30 min (m/30 min), and Daily Activity Rate (DAR, %). Calculate mean values (DDT ≈ 1 760.7 m/day, Speed ≈ 42.8 m/30 min, DAR ≈ 40.1 %) and compare with values over the entire monitoring period (DDT ≈ 1 974 m/day, Speed ≈ 47.0 m/30 min, DAR ≈ 40.1 %). Fit Generalized Additive Mixed Models (GAMMs) with explanatory variables: post‑capture period, season, sex, monitoring zone, outdoor temperature (°C), and time of day; retain post‑capture delay only for DAR (significant reduction in activity during the first month).

steps.title: Perform spatial and habitat analyses
steps.instruction: Map all telemetry points; construct home ranges using MCP 100 % and Kernel Density Estimators (KDE 95 % and KDE 50 %). Build a “monitoring zone” categorical variable by calculating an Artificialisation Index (AI) and a Human Disturbance Index (DI) from six and three land‑cover criteria respectively (e.g., forest cover %, road density, building density, land‑cover diversity, etc.). Use the regional Nouvelle‑Aquitaine land‑cover database (fine resolution) and the French topographic database (2020) for distances to roads and buildings. Apply QGIS “FragScape” plugin with Cross‑Boundaries Connection to compute forest fragmentation (CBC‑MSIZ). Assign each boar’s home range to one of three zones (Jalles, Periurban, Entre‑deux‑mers) based on summed (+) and (‑) scores for AI and DI as described in Table 1.
